name: Behistun Inscription
info: The Behistun Inscription is a multilingual Achaemenid royal inscription and rock relief on a cliff in Kermanshah Province, Iran, made for Darius the Great, and the longest known trilingual cuneiform text, central to the decipherment of cuneiform.

facts.made: Authored by Darius the Great, king of the Achaemenid Empire, sometime between his coronation in the summer of 522 BCE and his death in autumn 486 BCE
facts.form: A rock relief and trilingual cuneiform inscription in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, about 15 metres high and 25 metres wide: 414 lines in five columns in Old Persian, 260 lines in eight columns in Elamite and 112 lines in Babylonian
facts.where: On a limestone cliff at Mount Behistun (Bisotun), near Kermanshah in western Iran, about 100 metres above an ancient road between Babylon and Ecbatana; an Aramaic copy of the text was found in Egypt
facts.known: the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription; the key to deciphering Old Persian cuneiform; Darius's account of his ancestry and of nineteen battles in a year; the list of twenty-three subject lands; the relief of Darius and the bound rebels; Henry Rawlinson's climb to copy it; UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2006

t: Darius the Great had the text carved on a cliff above the road between Babylon and Ecbatana. It gives his ancestry, lists the lands he ruled and recounts nineteen battles fought in one year against rebels and impostors.
It is the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, and this made it important to the decipherment of cuneiform.

Forgotten for centuries and explained in fanciful ways, it was copied by travellers and scholars from 1598 onward, and Henry Rawlinson sent a full and accurate copy of the Old Persian text to Europe in 1847.
dyk: Darius's beard on the relief is a separate block of stone attached with iron pins and lead, and one of the nine bound figures appears to have been added after the others were finished.

sections.origins:
The inscription belongs to the reign of Darius the Great (r. 522–486 BCE), who was crowned king of the Achaemenid Empire in the summer of 522 BCE. It stands on Mount Behistun in Kermanshah Province, near the city of Kermanshah in western Iran. The Old Persian name of the place was Bagastana, meaning "the place of god". The cliff rises above an ancient road that connected the capitals of Babylonia and Media, Babylon and Ecbatana, so that travellers on one of the main routes of the region passed beneath it.

The place had a long history before Darius. Archaeological evidence indicates that the region became a human shelter 40,000 years ago, and the Behistun complex covers 116 hectares. The relief also had models. The Anubanini rock relief at Sarpol-e Zahab, made for the Lullubi king Anubanini and dated to about 2300 BCE, lies not far away and resembles it closely in the attitude of the ruler, the trampling of an enemy and the lines of prisoners. It is speculated that the sculptors of Behistun had probably seen it, and the Lullubian reliefs are described as the model for Darius's. The inscriptional tradition of the Achaemenids, especially from Darius I, is thought to derive from the traditions of Elam, Lullubi, the Babylonians and the Assyrians.
sections.content:
The inscription opens with a brief autobiography of Darius, in which he names his father Hystaspes and traces his descent through Arsames, Ariaramnes and Teispes to Achaemenes. He states that this is why the family are called Achaemenids, that eight of his dynasty were kings before him and that he is the ninth, and that by the grace of Ahuramazda he is king. A later passage lists the countries subject to him, twenty-three lands in all, from Persia, Elam, Babylonia and Assyria to Egypt, Lydia, the Greeks, Media, Bactria, Sogdia, Gandhara and Scythia.

The longest part is an account of the events that followed the death of Cambyses II. Darius states that he fought nineteen battles in one year, ending in December 521 BCE, to put down rebellions across the empire. In his account the revolts were organised by several impostors and their co-conspirators in various cities, each of whom falsely proclaimed himself king. Darius presents himself as victorious in every battle and credits his success to the grace of Ahura Mazda.

The text is illustrated by a life-sized bas-relief of Darius holding a bow as a sign of kingship, with his left foot on the chest of a figure lying on its back, reputed to be the pretender Gaumata. Two servants attend him on the left. On the right stand nine one-metre figures with hands tied and ropes round their necks, representing conquered peoples, and a Faravahar floats above, giving its blessing to the king.
sections.making:
Darius authored the inscription sometime between his coronation in the summer of 522 BCE and his death in the autumn of 486 BCE. It is written in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, a variety of Akkadian. The Old Persian text has 414 lines in five columns, the Elamite text 260 lines in eight columns and the Babylonian text 112 lines. The whole composition, text and relief, measures about 15 metres in height and 25 metres in width, and it was cut into a limestone cliff about 100 metres above the road.

The relief shows signs of having been altered during the work. One of the nine bound figures appears to have been added after the others were completed, and so was Darius's beard, which is a separate block of stone attached with iron pins and lead. The inscription depicts no battle directly and describes the campaigns with a formulaic brevity. As in earlier inscriptions, it stresses the connection between victory and divine approval, and its selective geographical patterns, dates and statistics serve to enhance its credibility. A copy of the text in Aramaic, written during the reign of Darius II, was found in Egypt.
sections.reception:
After the fall of the Achaemenid dynasty and its successors, and after Old Persian cuneiform fell out of use, the nature of the inscription was forgotten and fanciful explanations became the norm. The name Behistun comes from Ancient Greek and Arabic sources, in particular Diodorus Siculus and Ya'qubi, and was transliterated into English in the 19th century by Henry Rawlinson. The modern Persian name is Bisotun.

In 1598 the Englishman Robert Sherley saw the monument during a diplomatic mission to Safavid Persia on behalf of Austria and brought it to the attention of Western European scholars. His party wrongly concluded that it was Christian in origin. The French general Gardanne thought it showed Christ and his twelve apostles, and Sir Robert Ker Porter thought it represented the Lost Tribes of Israel and Shalmaneser of Assyria. In 1604 the Italian explorer Pietro della Valle visited and made preliminary drawings.

Scholarly study followed. Carsten Niebuhr, a German surveyor travelling for Frederick V of Denmark, visited around 1764 and published a copy in 1778. Georg Friedrich Grotefend and others used his transcriptions in trying to decipher Old Persian cuneiform, and by 1802 Grotefend had deciphered ten of its 37 symbols, after realising that Old Persian, unlike the Semitic cuneiform scripts, is alphabetic and separates its words with a slanted vertical sign.
sections.survival:
The inscription has survived on its cliff, but its condition has changed. Rainwater has dissolved some areas of the limestone in which the text was cut, while leaving new deposits of limestone over other areas and covering the text. In the 20th century the monument suffered some damage from Allied soldiers using it for target practice in the Second World War and during the Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran. In 1938 the Nazi German think tank Ahnenerbe took an interest in the inscription, but its research plans were cancelled because of the outbreak of the war.

Rawlinson began studying it in earnest in 1835 and, with the help of a local boy, scaled the cliff despite its relative inaccessibility to copy the Old Persian text. The Elamite lay across a chasm and the Babylonian four metres above, both beyond easy reach, and he left them for later. A British Museum expedition in 1904, led by Leonard William King and Reginald Campbell Thompson, and a University of Michigan expedition in 1948 under George G. Cameron obtained photographs, casts and more accurate transcriptions, including passages that Rawlinson had not copied.

In 1999 Iranian archaeologists began to document and assess the damage of the 20th century, using photogrammetry with two cameras to make three-dimensional images. Conservation work followed, and the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006. In 2012 the Bisotun Cultural Heritage Center organised an international effort to re-examine the inscription.
sections.legacy:
The inscription became important to the decipherment of cuneiform because it is the longest known trilingual cuneiform text. The same account stands in three languages, and the Old Persian version, which Rawlinson copied and sent in full to Europe in 1847, gave scholars a text they could work from. Because the town's name was anglicised as Behistun at the time Rawlinson began his study in 1835, the monument became known as the Behistun Inscription.

Its text is also a source for the history of the early reign of Darius. It records the ancestry he claimed, the lands he ruled and his own version of the rebellions after the death of Cambyses II. Scholars have continued to study it, with new readings and editions published in recent years of its Elamite version and of one of its paragraphs, and with one hypothesis that treats it as an imperial calendar.

The Behistun complex holds eighteen other historical monuments registered in the Iranian national list of historical sites. Paul J. Since its listing as a World Heritage Site in 2006 the inscription has remained a subject of conservation and research.

summary: The Behistun Inscription is a trilingual rock inscription and relief that Darius the Great had cut into a cliff in western Iran, recounting his ancestry and his nineteen battles against rebels in one year. It was copied by European travellers and scholars from 1598 and was important to the decipherment of cuneiform.
